Exactly. His electric math is wrong too.

Electric motors generally range from 80%-98% efficient. The very high end generally become cost prohibitive but that price is likely to come down if widely adopted for electric vehicles. The result is that most of the motors used tend to be roughly 94% efficient.

What further complicates things is that most electric cars are not direct drive. They still go through a basic transmission. Usually this is to allow for the use of multiple motors. This mechanical transmission is generally 90% efficient.

Electricity delivery has improved over the years. In most places within the US electricity is delivered at 90-95% efficiency.

Lastly, this power must be stored in batteries. A Li-on battery, when new, has 99% efficiency.

0.94 * 0.9 * 0.9 * 0.9 * 0.99 = 68% efficient. But let's be crazy conservative and say 60%.

Most ICE average around 26% - 30% efficiency to the ground. But let's say we exclude things like trucks, which moves us into the 30% range. Clearly the winner is the electric vehicle. It's not even close. Even if we assume much more loss in efficiency batteries over time and the mechanical transmission.

What everyone loves to ignore is a pragmatic reality of how engines and motors are used. ICE requires RPMs to build to generate torque. Electric motors have high torque as soon as they begin to turn. Which means electric motors use less energy to provide the same driving habits.

Also, many people here are parroting what is known as range anxiety. 80% of the US population can satisfy their driving habits today with an electric vehicle. For Europe, this is 90% of the drivers. This is because, on average, the vast majority of a driver's daily distance is less than the total capacity of a battery pack. You simply charge at night, during off peak hours.

Additionally, as some others have provided, electric vehicles also allow for centralized production of energy. Energy production costs for gas is very high where as energy production costs for nuclear fuel is rather low in comparison. But we can accept this as simple a measure of it's cost. Gas prices are volatile and high relative to nuclear's stable and low. Also, there is no cleaner source of energy than nuclear currently in mass use. Electric vehicles can run off of nuclear power.

Without any question, in every measure, electric vehicles are superior. The only thing which prevents from being superior to every application is battery density and (refuel) charge time. There are several very interesting developments which may leave the lab soon which allow for 80% charge time in roughly five minutes. Getting that much power to a charge station is a different question. But to some degree this may also be facilitate by super capacitor charging banks.

A gasoline internal combustion engine has about 20% thermal efficiency (how much energy is actually converted of the available energy). Modern improvements push that to closer to 50% under certain circumstances, but more like 40% in real use case.

A steam power plant based on a Rankine cycle is about 75% efficient in converting the thermal source to electrical energy. A/C power transmission over the grid is around 90% efficient (85-95% depending on use case), and electrical motors are around 90% efficient (less when starting, regain power when stopping as they can recoup mechanical energy into battery, as high as 98% while cruising). .9 * .9 * .75 = 60.75%. An electric vehicle charging from the grid off an oil power plant is 1.5-3x more effective in converting that energy source to kinetic force than an internal combustion engine burning the same fuel.

You can build a steam vehicle, they were doing it into the 1950s, but the reality is starting and stopping the engine wastes a large amount of energy where little to no work can be done. You have to heat the system to its operating temp, and you have to let it cool without collecting any of that energy, or you leave it burning when no work is being done.

This means that yes, by far the most efficient system in use today is to charge an electric vehicle from the grid. To Anything that could improve that without compromising vehicle performance would require a wholly new and disruptive technology.

What you're looking for is to use element hiding rules instead of using network filters. With these, the network requests all go through, and then after the page loads the object is removed, just as though you had hit F12, selected it and hit delete. In ublock origin these filters are preceded by ##, as opposed to network filters which begin ||.

The top adblockers support element hiding rules, but most filter lists prefer network filters as they're more secure and private. There may be something like a ublock origin fork pre-configured for this, or possibly a custom list that only includes element hiding rules. If you can't find a dedicated product for it, a two-blocker solution could make the whole thing easier: set up one adblocker, say ublock, set it up normally, and whitelist the sites you want to. Then set up a second, say adblock plus, give it a list with only element hiding rules, then have that one enabled all the time. Theoretically this would make it as simple as hitting the power button on ubo when you wanted to do this.

You might still need anti-anti-adblock for this on some sites which use a script fired a while after the page loads to check if the element is visible to trigger their anti-adblock. IMO a site that does shit like that doesn't deserve whitelisting at all, but you can make that choice for yourself.
